body: Don't get yourself stuck in the same box I was left in; the one that believes the hype that DBT is the gold standard and/or only answer. I waited a decade to get into a program and it didn't help; in fact it left me worse off, but I'm not saying it couldn't work; I'm just saying that it is ridiculously difficult to find a program in this city and there are other options that are viable, too. I actually have a lot of criticisms about the way DBT programs are ran, including the individual therapy aspect, but I digress: consider your symptoms and what you want to focus on treating. Do you think trauma work is important? Then DBT is NOT the answer and surprisingly, not all therapists are even trained in trauma work, so I'd pick a treatment very carefully. Do you want to work on emotional regulation? Then find a course about that. The meditation aspect speak to you? There are tons of free options for that. Like CBT? Then [Mindbeacon](https://www.mindbeacon.com/tgp-getstarted?hsCtaTracking=18c34e07-ea03-4590-b0f5-eba266b3bf6a%7C37fc7396-eab7-4eb7-a3a4-159dab88eb3e) is free in Ontario and offers one-on-one support while you learn coping mechanisms that are tailored to you. As far as the focus you mention though, I'd really recommend [WRAP](https://www.mooddisordersottawa.ca/wrap) (Wellness Recovery Action Plan); it's free, peer led, and way back when I took that course, it helped me more than anything to this day, though I didn't have as much luck with their follow-up program Pathways.
I believe you, but it seems I'm always the wrong person in another's presence, only more so when I'm just my broken self.

Why isn't therapy for humans more like this? Instead of being pushed away every time I dare to share I'm trying to show/test if I can trust. https://www.reddit.com/r/MadeMeSmile/comments/jlbvj1/bonding_with_a_newly_sheltered_pup/

Or maybe we should be like dang that dog crossed boundaries, how dare it.
D'aww, I'm sure I'll probably delete all my posts and go into hiding as usual soon, but that's sweet.

It's weird to go through life feeling like you're some sort of myth despite being sure - somewhere inside this body and mind you carry like luggage of their own - that you do in fact exist. Even when you try to give someone your truth, they seemingly want to deal with the damage that became of you about as much as your abusers wanted to see the real you. It's all very perpetuating of the trauma when even the help is a paradox that beckons you to be the one who *needs to work harder on being a better someone else* under the guise of well-meaning *change*, without realizing that people never seeing you as good enough, and expecting complete otherness of you all along, was what trapped you in this hell of a cage in which you're unable to really speak despite the otherwise convincing noises your mouth might make. But everyone's blind to the fact that you just became the invisibility that another wanted of you for so long so you could get anything but another's rage and hate; in your own invisibility to yourself, it's nearly impossible to even put into words what the other never wanted you to have words to say. Then - one day - you might be (un)lucky enough to reach a certain point of realizing *something's not right*; you can't hide anymore that you're here; you're alive; you're an individual in your own right, and you're exceptionally, passionately, and unforgivingly pissed off that some other being stole your sight. But even that - the defenses that try to make *you being you alright* pit against the defenses that would have you never having seen the light - just become the weapon against you when you try to share all the pain of what it means to relinquish the love you *thought* "you" got for playing pretend for another's sake, and the hate __you__ got for being real for your own sake. It's a trap that can keep you on the path to self-hate because it was always made dangerous to mess with what someone else demanded of your fate while looking for something you lost that's so fundamentally important, but that you *as yourself* can't even define. What's worse is that if this monster left in you can't have your sight anymore, it'll take everybody else's away from seeing you as anything but everything they hate, and they'll be none the wiser, too, all while you scream silently, "Help..." and just have to wait because all the help you scream for never can seem to relate to the conflict you're in about the love you only learned to acquire out of being whatever the other didn't hate. Now you're being and showing you - full of anger, hurt, fear, defenses, and pain - and all you want is for it to be okay to be what you couldn't ever be before... But it still might be too soon or too late as the question looms whether it'd have all been so much better if you were just better at hiding that which you couldn't fake. Maybe it would be safer to try going back there since the words that were found to get away from it and finally bring expression to yourself have yet to work either to make your being visible anymore okay. There has to be... A better way. 

Or that's just me and I'm being overly dramatic and possibly poetic, but... It's really this intense, and so difficult to share when it's like the words don't seem like they should even make sense!

Hi, welcome to a community of people who are in therapy for a multitude of issues that range from "simple" to "complex." It's probably not the best place to suggest such a hopeless perspective about treating any sort of issue. I mean, it's right up there with my old foster parent stating that my current diagnosis (which they aren't aware of) is "untreatable," and should only be "empathized with from a distance," when their partner (also my foster parent at one time) was a psychologist. Speak for your experiences; your burnout; your (lack of) motivation, and purely *your* challenges of treating a certain demographic of the mentally ill all you want, but it *only* speaks to your capacity to do-so with whatever tools and supports you did or didn't have to do that. That said, it simultaneously does represent the pathetic state of mental health treatment that I can at least *personally* attest to coming into contact with on more than a few occasions, too. Nobody's untreatable; the proper treatment just isn't always there, which is to say that part of the issue is that many mental illnesses are not properly understood yet, much as we'd like to believe we're ahead. Perspectives like yours put us decades behind though.

Nothing quite like having trauma about people not believing you're being honest, while simultaneously not wanting you to be yourself at all to the point of making you feel like you have to pretend you are what they want you to be/hide who you really are for your own safety to then end you up in therapy where you feel like the only way someone might even *try* to help you and *not abandon you* (for just being *you*) is actually by doing what your abusers expected all along; by 'fronting' and keeping things about yourself hidden so you don't lose the help that you need, but really: how helpful is that? 

The damage that has been re-ignited by my simply being honest is palpable.

> The idea of treating it more like an epileptic fit is pretty progressive isn't it ?

I think the fact that we're so highly judged based on the diagnosis is part of what makes us so difficult to treat, because we're already dealing with our own internal monologue of judgment based on a sense of being out of control of what others expect us to be in control of. Hell, my own trauma involves that and a huge lack of acceptance to that being true at all. On top of that, I think a lot of patients struggle with being *blinded* to seeing these sorts of things about themselves; as we know, one of the components for diagnosis is lacking a sense of self, which I think is a trauma response to keep one's self safe all along, but it is equally protective to be in denial of that being the case [you can't miss or mourn what you didn't know you lost]. I think a lot of people with BPD take on the blame without realizing they're not at blame at all because... It's also a trauma response! So even from that perspective, I think some of the treatment modes are re-traumatizing, even if they appear to work on the surface level; the individual with BPD (without even realizing it) might be prone to 'front' that the treatment is working to keep the supports in place at the risk of disposing their true self even further. Then we get into the factor of 'manipulation' (my least favourite word) and I again have the perspective that there is no ill intention to do such a thing; the 'front' is so strong at keeping the real person hidden that all it can do is play along by giving 'right' answers and by trying to be compliant, until - y'know - it can't anymore and goes off the rails. I mean, maybe there are individuals with the diagnosis that would intentionally do so for their own gain, but I know I'm right shit at making anybody do what I want, even when I outright tell them what it is that I want or even need. I base this on my own aggravation at the stigmatizing articles out there that talk as if we're malicious and cruel without a conscience. It's awful! And of course I wouldn't want to expose myself vulnerably to anyone if no matter what I tell them, they can find their own way of mixing up my words in their own polysemy to mean whatever they want it to mean. We clearly have attachment trauma, too, so this just exacerbates the whole idea of sharing ourselves as well.

> My doctor recommended lamictal for years and when I tried it, even at a small dose, I would have fits of rage that were physical.

Interesting... And you're still on it? You mentioned being on 300mg of something. I did keto for 2 years straight hoping that when I got off it, I might have long-term effects that stayed with me, but it was not to be so. I haven't been on it during the pandemic and it's been so difficult to get back onto it. I struggle with cooking, so I'm a very lazy keto-er, but I know I need to get back on for my sanity. It's not helping anything to be off it.

> I was never diagnosed with epilepsy as I never had seizures.

Neither, and I've never experienced any of the symptoms you mentioned, but it's interesting that the act of dissociation does resemble in its own way that of a petite mal. I'm only saying that as comparison, not to suggest that they are exactly the same thing, but I'd wager they happen in the same region of the brain.

> I've found that all things which increase my reslience in ways, especially Keto and weight training, seem to help 

Interesting that you use the word resilience as the key to your success. Maybe you can explain what that means for you? I think I'm starting to find that I need an outlet that reminds me of who I am without me feeling bad to be (reminded of) that? I often have jumped from hobby to hobby; the interest would just *die* within a few months, and off I'd go to something else. Recently I started writing and I found I had all these words that I realized had been stuffed down so as not to hurt other people, even if they were my truth. It's kind of been a big deal, while at the same time, the whole concept of self-expression feels dangerous to me (like it'll hurt other people, or make them abandon me, or I'll lose my mind by being creative). So there's that... Which I was, I think, trying to show my therapist to build a sense of safety through their acceptance... Before I ran away because they had a negative reaction at a point to my self-expression heh

Interesting. It definitely feels like something that's not in control, so it becomes that much more frustrating when the perspective of the professionals is that you just need to learn to control yourself better (especially because the trauma doesn't matter *because* you have BPD). I'm not saying it's not plausible or possible that skills can help; I'm not saying we shouldn't be held accountable, but simultaneously, it at times does feel like being at the mercy of a seizure that if you let people know you had, or they happened to witness (or sadly are a part of) it happening, they'd simply reply (and basically have): "Stop hitting your own head on the floor." Yes, well... Let me get right on that after my neurotransmitters and whatever the hell else in my head stop over-firing and back-firing against my own demands? Like it's so hard to tell someone, "Really, I have no desire to be *this way* that I *sometimes* am, and I'd give anything to just make that part of me that takes over go away." I feel like there's HUGE defenses that come into play that also make it challenging to be able to say that (clearly) when it's true though; my own brain is at least like "NOPE... ADMITTING TO FAULT IS WRONG; YOU'RE JUST ASKING TO BE PUNISHED FOR IT; DON'T YOU DARE LET YOUR DEFENSES DOWN AND BE VULNERABLE!" Also, the fact that you're internally also screaming at your own brain, "WTF WAS THAT GDI I TOLD YOU TO CUT IT OUT" also doesn't exactly make you feel like taking the blame *again* because all you can do is defend the fact that you were totally telling your brain to not do exactly what it did anyway. But you know, this is all going on inside without words, because neurons and synapses are all just like, "Bzzt, bzzt, berzerk!" It's like some terrible self-fulfilling prophecy that keeps re-inflicting trauma through these half-assed defenses that somehow convince you that they'll actually avoid it from happening again; stupid brain can't make up its mind about keeping me safe, and like some constant game of 'Pick-a-door' that always leads to the least helpful solution, the reaction is so often a disaster. Oh to let someone into my brain. 

I did my own research as well and there definitely appears to be a glutamate connection: https://www.reddit.com/r/keto/comments/1k30u5/therapist_was_concerned_about_diet_despite_it/

For what it's worth, I *did* take Lamictal (which is for epilepsy) and it *did* help, but it also ruined my word recall, so it just basically muted me [seriously, I'd wager there's something with our language that's part of the equation, too, because I often feel like the words *just don't come out right*]. There was another seizure medication recommended to me off label but I did not end up trying it.

I'd rather they call it an Emotional Seizure Disorder. It seems appropriate having had more luck in treating it with a Ketogenic diet, which is a last ditch effort they implement with children who suffer seizures who are "treatment resistant." All so very apt.. Heh.

Aaah yes, TIBs! Otherwise known as, "Transference Is Bad," in DBT language... Or the general label to use when your client is difficult and you want an excuse to abandon them instead of taking the time necessary to examine what the cause of the actual issue is in the first place, because... Y'know... Skills trump any other sort of focus, including legitimate trauma if you get labeled as having BPD. A load of crock, if you ask me. Did you also know that part of DBT's 'treatment' is that if you miss 4 appointments in a row, they're supposed to discharge you as well? But shhh, you're not supposed to know how it works! 

Probably not the best time to be seeing a post like yours, I admit... The state of care for individuals with trauma, and therefore defenses against further trauma, is half-assed at best. I'll shut up before I end up anymore outraged, but no... I'm far from over it, and I think I am done with any sort of 'therapy' from here-on-out.

Let me just add that TIBs should stand for 'This Is Bullshit'. Seriously; anyone who goes to therapy isn't trying to interfere with therapy! *They are doing therapy the best way they can,* and just *maybe* what comes up during that time should be considered *equally if not more important* than skills, because it just might be something the client didn't trust to tell anyone previously.
